comments.body: The program would save a lot by pushing back the eligibility age, since people live longer today than they did in FDR's day.  When the program began in 1940, average life expectancy of a  male born that year was 70 years, and the age of eligibility for full benefits was 65.  In 86 years since then, the eligibility age has only been pushed back two years, while male life expectancy has added 12 years.  That's an additional ten more years of benefits than initially intended.

The dots have been connected. In the public eye obscene wealth has been finally been directly linked to graft and corruption. Its charming innocence has been lost. When this happens, massive oligarchic spending on campaign advertising begins to backfire. It no longer dazzles and sways the gullible masses. It now constitutes proof that the critics of oligarchical abuse and control were right all along. 

The fact that the noble illusion of the American Dream is rapidly fading from sight further fuels the process. Honesty and hard work no longer seem to pay off. The crooks and grifters are seen to have their hands in every pot. This means that highly visible possession of great wealth has suddenly become tainted, more a sign of criminality than of virtue.

T Michael White MD

Just a comment pn North African immigrants living in the same neighborhoods. The first Americans in my family came to Wisconsin in the 1850s. Had they done  careful research on agricultural productivity before choosing that area? Had they looked into the cost of transportation from New York City?   Maybe so, but who did they find in northern Wisconsin? Many, many, many other Germans. comments.name: Livonian
comments.body:
I saw the “Age of Grievance” attitude grow among young people over my 30 year career at UCLA from which I recently retired.

In my work I hired and supervised many students, all ambitious.  But I noticed as the years passed by that every consecutive batch of students seemed a bit less capable of handling ordinary life challenges and setbacks, were more eager to complain, to ask authorities to intervene, to plead for special treatment.  I actually had a young man tell me he couldn’t make deliveries to the lab, the main focus of his job, because the smell of meat emanating from the cafeteria “overwhelmed” him as a strict vegan.

But worse, there was this growing sense that any ordinary friction in life was unfair, proof that something had gone wrong “out there” with “the System,” and that only when the System was fixed, could the challenge be overcome.  The jungle path had to be cleared ahead of them by others before they could proceed.

Terrifying.  On the other hand, I did encounter some absolutely stellar young people on occasion, and I found they tended to come from more humble backgrounds.

The federal budget deficit for FY 2026 is $1.992 trillion, between 6.0% and 6.2% of your country's GDP.  (The federal budget deficit for FY 2025 was $1.775 trillion.)

comments.name: Felix
comments.body:
I dont think the nations we have are going to "fail" in the same way we consider, say, Somalia as a failed state. But thanks to the decisions of those who came before us, most the boomer generation since Reagan, we have a huge debt crisis looming.

The US has a debt that is accounting for 14% of the government budget every year, trending RAPIDLY upwards. France and the UK have a similar problem with increasingly swiftly growing debt piles with no serious effort to get it under control. A big part of that is that the generations before ours took out this debt and used it to subsidize their own life and pay for their own healthcare and social services and we are expected to say "oh okay, we will pay off that debt for you and in return have none of those services because you didn't set them up in a sustainable manner". Of course people will revolt because cutting back will hurt, but it will hurt those who didnt benefit from it.

I can fully understand the extreme pessimism from my generation. We have only known a world where the cost of the basics move further and further out of reach each year, wealth consolidates in the hands of fewer and fewer people, and the opportunities to find employment routinely collapsing preventing you from starting your life. I am 26 years old and I have born the consequences for 4 different economic crises in my life time caused nearly exclusively by the boomer generation and gen x as they made up the dominant political forces for most of that time.

The countries shut down and we could not have entered the country if we had wanted to. Airbnb did not refund a single cent even when a host directed them to do so. Airbnb did not answer the phone and did not respond to my letter.

So, we paid for something that we were not allowed to use because of quarantines. Airbnb protected the hosts but ignored the renters. We lost several thousand dollars and, of course, our travel insurance did not cover pandemics. Who knew?

Going forward, we stay in hotels now, don't do any chores and get refundable room reservations. I think the company has forgotten why it began and has metastasized to the point where locals cannot find or afford housing anywhere near tourist sites.  To each their own but for us, we are over Airbnb.

Lots of salient points in the comments that I'll second. My husband and I have used AirB&B since they started, and like others, have had many wonderful experiences and met wonderful people.

However, in the last few years since Covid, a lot of hosts seem to have taken advantage of the "deep-cleaning" they continue to charge guests for, in addition to requiring us to do chores.

My husband and I are extremely tidy, clean guests--most hosts comment that "You couldn't tell Mr. and Mrs. -- had even stayed here; the house was spotless when they left." Since we're already conscientious guests, and since we're paying quite a bit of money to stay at these properties, we find it extremely distasteful to arrive at our rental house and find a list of chores that we're expected to do before we leave. We're on vacation! We're paying guests! We should not have to perform household chores. (Are they willing to refund part of our fee if we agree to do chores??)  Also, as another commenter stated, not everyone washes dishes thoroughly; it's disgusting to notice a dish is dirty as you're about to use it because a host wasn't willing to pay a housekeeper to clean thoroughly and, instead, expected guests to do grudgingly do the work. 

We still use AirB&B, but we now always ask before booking if we're going to be expected to do their chores for them. If they respond with a list, we find someplace else. 
Really glad to hear that this change is being made.

I host a 5-bdr Airbnb home and agree with the policy change.  I don't charge my guests for cleaning, but mostly limit their obligations.  Dishes were an exception, but Airbnb let me know this morning that expecting this was no longer an option -- and I'm fine with that.

As for being an Airbnb guest, I've learned it's great benefit is multi-unit living for groups -- not solo or couple travelers.  In that situation, who wants to get on their co-habitants case about the dishes?

One of those experiences was so mutually good that the host gave us his phone number to bypass Airbnb for future stays.  The other was good enough that we'd do it again through the platform.

Travel insurers typically have their own services for booking flights/evacuations and can often book upgrades or alternative flights for you - which means they pay the cost upfront. Putting aside how bizarre it is for a grown man to celebrate his birthday, I found that display sufficient to cut all ties. 

(2) Out to dinner with friend and his husband. Bar tab comes and everyone stares. Absolute silence. I put down my card and conversation resumes. They’re good people, but the entitlement was extremely offputting. 

The takeaway is two fold: what you think are just generous displays of affection might end up being the worst thing you can do for your friendship in the long term—the expectation builds resentment on both side. Second, your friends’ finances aren’t your responsibility; they’re adults and it’s on them to say “Sorry, things are a little tight this month. How about we just have some wine on the patio instead?”

They are exceedingly expensive to keep, several hundred a month for board, trims and perhaps shoes every 6 to 8 weeks, another several hundred a year and biannual vet visits which is another $1,000/yr. Not to mention anything you might need if you want to ride, very expensive sport. These owners love their animals and they get the best care for their animals. One death in 100 years? comments.name: BL
comments.body:
The working horses have owners who care about them. "Rescues" cannot just take them nor can the city prohibit their transfer or determine what happens to the horses after the carriages are gone. 

New York City does not have the legal standing to regulate interstate commerce nor do they have the right to stipulate what happens to privately-owned livestock outside of their municipality.  

It is a poorly written bill and its claims that the horses can never work again anywhere and can never be slaughtered are just empty words to win a few City Council votes from people who really don't know a thing about horses. It is all simply political cover. Nothing more. 

If the bill passes, everyone who voted for it will forget about the horses and the workers employed in the carriage trade in a New York minute. 

Yes, NYC can end carriages. That's an administrative rule change. 

But as for the horses? Many will end their lives at slaughter if their owners are put out work and their businesses shut down by the city.

There are already over 20,000 horses, mule and donkeys that cannot find homes and get shipped to Mexico and Canada for slaughter. Those are the ones that need "saving," not the carriage horses.

They could look like drawings or have a watermark that wasn't taken off.  Along with AI photos, AI videos can be even easier to spot. AI videos have fake voices and have that same art style as AI videos. Since the videos have the same art style it also helps with spotting AI generated photos. comments.name: Kai Cenat
comments.body:
Have You Ever Been Fooled by an A.I.-Generated Photo, Video or Story?
 I have fallen for an AI photo and it was actually pretty recent. About two weeks ago there was a Tornado that had struck down here damaging many buildings and even flipping cars all around the town. We were under warnings all throughout North Carolina and many places were affected by this storm. Soon later after the storm had passed A very helpful social media account called Watchout 910 had reported all the places that were affected along with the damage the storm had done all over. I had noticed a very popular post going around the platform, Instagram which had shown a picture of the Tornado itself. The comments were all skeptical debating whether it was real or not as most people would be taking cover along with how the photo just looks a bit fake. AI makes it very difficult to be able to determine if something is real or fake with how much it has advanced. Later on I came to the realization that the photo was fake after Watchout 910 had declared it as 100% AI. I feel like our generation has become a bit half and half on believe what we all see. There are times when a photo/video is so obvious to be fake yet many people still believe it's real because it's "Popular" or everyone is saying it is. You can even run these photos, Videos or posts  through  AI scanners but people don't want to put in that extra work so they just leave it alone.

Having those people become comfortable to the fact that a gay man's voice fills their homes (via Fox News) on a daily basis. A veteran, a rhodes scholar, a Harvard graduate, and beyond. 

But there's still so many unknowns to getting there, and a senate win for Pappas will certainly help. Pete is the best guy for the job for 2028 - let's figure out how to navigate the details. Go Pappas!

comments.name: Caps
comments.body:
Really interesting to see so many commenters recoil from this headline because it vaguely reminds them of phrenology. 

It makes me wonder whether researchers over the last several decades might have unconsciously avoided studying intracranial geometry so as to avoid any associations with phrenology's racist associations.

People very strongly connect phrenology with "race science" - rightly so, because phrenology was used by some to support discredited, racist theories. And the central theory of phrenology - that someone's mental traits can be inferred by observable measurements of the outside of the skull - has been debunked.

But there were many well-meaning and non-racist 19th century scientists who explored phrenology purely in the spirit of medical advancement. Their overarching theory was misguided, but they helped to advance some discoveries that we now take for granted - e.g. establishing that a human's mental functions arise from a brain located inside the skull and that different areas of the brain are responsible for different functions. 

It was a stepping stone on the path to greater enlightenment.

Here are three main factors contributing to a collapse in government and public sector finances in many countries:

1. Government led programs that simply do not pay for themselves. Those include military spending and pension and other welfare programs.

2. Short sighted and sometimes corrupt politicians and government officials. They operate with no fiscal guardrails or responsibility. The people in charge have no accountability for generating public sector income, except imposing and raising taxes. Voting a politician out of office solves nothing. They simply depart and collect a nice pension.

3. A voting public with a mindset focused on their own often limited pocket book. Day to day lives of the average citizen is a scramble to make ends meet. It creates an inherent disconnect between individual fiscal responsibility and public policy. It’s an ever spinning greed over need conundrum.

To start correcting the current financial stresses in many western democracies, one or more of the above issues must be addressed.

The Weaponization of AI

China’s restriction of foundational AI exports—like high-parameter large models and source code—marks a monumental shift. AI has officially transitioned from an open commercial frontier into a tightly guarded instrument of national security.

1. State Power Over Free Markets
While the U.S. pioneered tech export bans, Beijing’s new controls prove that great powers react identically when strategic assets are at stake. Just as Washington protects its hardware monopoly, Beijing is locking down its algorithmic crown jewels.

2. Offensive vs. Defensive Sovereignty

The U.S. approach has been offensive—using chip choke points to block a rival's rise.

The Chinese approach is defensive—permitting API access while banning the export of underlying model weights, balancing global reach with strict state oversight.

3. Fragmenting the Tech Commons
The casualty of these mutual restrictions is the globalized tech ecosystem. A unified AI community is fracturing into sovereign tech blocs, forcing third-party nations to navigate competing Washington and Beijing frameworks.

Conclusion
China’s AI controls expose the myth of free-market high-tech globalization. When a technology defines future dominance, realpolitik trumps free trade. National security reigns supreme.

Additionally, the application of mineral fiber fire resistive coatings, whether spray or trowel applied, results in coatings that can easily become dislodged when disturbed by maintenance workers, airflow from above ceiling ventilation systems, earthquake, or other events, such as in the tragic terrorist air attacks on the World Trade Center towers, thereby reducing efficacy and suffusing air inside buildings with potentially carcinogenic fibers that can be inhaled by people.  Lastly, intumescent paints can often be found applied on exposed structural steel within buildings for aesthetic reasons, such as at the Morgan Library in New York City. I grew up in an historic district.  When the side porch, which was not original to the house, began to be unsound, my parents wanted to have it removed and were told they could not--again, even though it was not original to the house.  Exasperated, they pointed out the safety hazard, and the board was unmoved.  Finally, they asked, "What if it falls down?"  That was apparently fine, and in such case, it would not have to be replaced because (once more for the cheap seats in the back) it was not original to the building.  

Common sense and removal of liability is apparently just too logical in many preservation cases.

comments.name: Robert Harper
comments.body: My wife and I raised our family in a National Register house in the historic district of St Augustine,FL. We lived in that city for fifty years. During that time I even served on the Historic Architectural Review Bd. Most property owners seemed willing to comply with the regulations and felt it was important to preserve the character and history of the district. In recent years these codes seemed to relax and it shows. Due to the escalation of property values families and other owners moved out of the neighborhoods only to be replaced by commercial interests establishing vacation rentals or Airbnbs. Corporations seem to turn a blind eye to authentic paint colors and unique historic construction details. Interior construction is not regulated. Keeping the outside of a building authentic is a small and reasonable price to pay for the privilege of living in important historic neighborhoods.

comments.body:
We’re heart deep in a collective Dark Night of the Soul. We’re being asked by the Cosmos to re-imagine Who we are as a species. Changing our habits and our technologies isn’t going to be enough. Life is demanding (less and less politely with every shuttered eye) that we reassess and fundamentally change our relationship with the Earth and Nature so that instead of being parasites on our host, we recognize that we, too, are “Nature”. Our illusion that we are separate from Nature and can bend her to our will and flaunt our dominion over her needs to dissolve.

Why won’t we act? Because we’ve forgotten how to Love. Our coral reefs are calling out to us in pain. Our rivers and lakes are drying up like our tears. We poison the sky, our living waters, the soils that feed us, our children’s futures — all without blinking. We’ve forgotten that the universe is a living organism worthy of Reverence. We’ve forgotten that we are all made of the same stuff — we are made of songbirds and honeybees, orcas and prairie grasses sifting and dancing on the wind — and they are made of us.

Yes, Love is hard work. And it takes courage to risk feeling the pain those beings we choose to Love feel, especially when we’re the source of that pain. But, even now, Mother Earth is showering us with her blessings. Time for us to return the favor. Whatever that costs us.

At one point one meteor streaked in so low and bright that most of us literally hit the deck.

comments.body: The downside is that it pulls people into the scourge of posting content, views, popularity contests and video editing and hours behind screens. Youtube can be helpful at times with "how to videos", but also highly destructive. I work in the behavioral health sciences. I continue to study the psychological impacts of social media. For example, half dressed women chopping wood or AI generated bear attacks. We already have an epidemic of loneliness and a fixation with "watching others" through our cocoon socially isolated lives. comments.name: Abigail
comments.body: Honestly, being a student of an early college high school is scary. While I do feel safer here than at my old school, walking around campus to get to my classes is an experience that chills me to the bones. At the high school building, we don't have many safety measures being taken; pretty much anyone can walk in and go as they please. On campus in general, there are a few police officers sitting watch, and of course there's campus security, but that doesn't seem to stop people from being made uncomfortable by others. And knowing that on campus, everyone can come and go is scary because you can experience things that change your entire view on the word and your surroundings.  I had an experience walking to and from my classes one day and I had someone following me the entire time. I was so scared I mentally froze and went on autopilot mode, just going between classes. While we do have law enforcement officers here on campus, I believe they don't make enough of an impact to make everyone feel one hundred percent safe. I feel like law enforcement officers should do more to ensure the safety of people so nobody should have to constantly check over their shoulders, be scared to listen to music while walking around, or even just anything like avoiding interacting  with others.

Do you think the presence of police officers on school campuses would make students and classrooms safer? I believe the presence makes the school Safer, as our school, CPHS (Cumberland Polytechnic), has no natural SROs in the school, but multiple Police Officers patroling and checking buildings, as one incident encouraged the increased level of Police on campus. On November 16, or around that time last year, two classmates, one being my middle school Friend, were struck by a speeding car as they were crossing the road, and the driver stated she couldn't see them from the sun glare. Ever since the accident, the College took the issue of pedestrian safety into its own hands, installing crossing lights and stationing multiple campus security officers to watch the crossing paths, as well as having police officers stop speeders or Parents stopping in the middle of the road to drop their kids off.

comments.name: Gavin

They should not only be there to intimidate students though they should also be a part of the school community to help the growing generation gain a  positive view on law enforcement. I do think having law enforcement on campus does make it safer for students as if there is a shooting or any other threat they are there and ready to respond. Having students be put through the justice system isn't necessarily a bad thing in my opinion because it teaches bad kids early on the real consequences of their action so they are less likely to do it again in the future and be stuck behind bars for many more years than they would for small charges. I do personally feel safe at school but I might have bias because I am a white male so I could see how people of color and women may feel unsafe at my school. The safety features we have in place to help prevent such scenarios are call buttons throughout campus to notify security of an incident and there are also cameras everywhere and safety officers that roam the campus. Our school does not have any dedicated law enforcement officers but there are typically one or two police cars on campus at any given time. I'm not sure of any specific impact that they have had at my time at the school but they do help slow down drivers by sitting at crosswalks to intimate any speeders or people that don't want to yield to pedestrians.

comments.name: John
comments.body:
What role, if any, should law enforcement have in schools? Do you think the presence of police officers on school campuses would make students and classrooms safer? Or, would it lead to negative consequences, such as more students swept into the justice system for minor offenses?

I believe that the role that law enforcement should have in schools is to serve as security. Having a law enforcement official like a police officer could help keep the school safe as they could provide additional security for the school. I feel like having police officers at school would make the place safer, the issue is the overabundance of officers. I feel like having one or two police officers serving as security at a school is fine but having multiple of them could cause two primary issues. The first issue is that it could make the students doubt the schools safety as having too much security could be a sign that the school is always having problems. The second issue with having multiple officers is that it people could see the additional security and get encouraged to cause more trouble as they could view the additional security as a challenge for them to overcome. On top of this officers also need to be mindful of what they arrest people for. Constantly arresting kids over the smallest issues just gives off the feeling that they can't handle the situation as instead of arresting someone for annually doing something dangerous they are arresting kids over tiny problems.

comments.name: Rose
comments.body: I feel as if law enforcement does, in fact, have a role in schools. Now, this may be controversial, and it might sound like I'm a goody-two-shoes, but I'd like you to hear me out. In some schools, violence has become so common that ISS is overcrowded. Clearly, that type of discipline isn't enough for those kids. Obviously, I'm aware that petty fistfighting shouldn't be enough to get a kid into the legal system, but I believe just having an officer at the school, just present, is enough to deter kids from doing harmful things. I personally feel a lot safer when law enforcement is on school grounds; even though I openly hate the cops, they still make me feel safer. Now, on the other hand, I believe sometimes it's way too far for law enforcement to intervene. That kid who kicked the principal should've been dealt with by the school instead of law enforcement. If police were involved every single time that a little kid put their hands on someone, then the cops would never get a break. It's not ok to ruin a kid's permanent record and potentially put their parents in financial ruin just because you think the cops are some sort of superhero for every minor problem.

comments.name: Grant DeKuiper
comments.body: I think it’s too much to say that law enforcement shouldn’t be in schools. Unfortunately in this day and age it’s far too common for someone to try and “speak their mind” through violence for zero police presence to be an option. That being said, I think there’s something to be said about possible negative consequences of constant prosecution of students and involving kids in the criminal justice system so early in their lives. The whole point of growing up is learning about how the world works and making mistakes so you can learn from them and grow up to be a better person. School teachers and administrators understand this and as result generally do a great job addressing bad behavior of students and doing it in a way where students learn from their mistakes but but aren’t afraid to make other mistakes and continue to learn. Law enforcement ignores a lot of the constructive process of growing up by using often harsh punishments for kids that aren’t bad people and creating anxiety about making mistakes and making a bad impression of law enforcement that results in more people growing up to be scared of it rather that trusting it to protect them. People who are put into the justice system are often looked down upon because people assume they’re these violent criminals, and now you’ve taken something that could’ve been solved by a principal and a detention to possibly ruining their future aspirations over a mistake they made just trying to grow up.

comments.name: Dana Thach
comments.body: Law enforcement in schools are necessary for various reasons: added layer of surveillance for students, safety for students against outside forces, potential issues with weapons, etc. With the mention of these reasons, pulling “tens of thousands of elementary students and middle schoolers into the justice system” is not valid based on the reasons of civil disputes such as “[slapping] another kid on the playground, [puffing] on a vape, or [kicking] a principal in frustration” (Sifton). It is notable to make aware that I don’t have much background with law or what is illegal and what is not. However, what I do know is that  detaining adolescents who still have developing minds is an action that will not change how they behave. Pulling children into a justice system and putting legal bills onto their family will only make them more frustrated and against change. An alternate route to changing troubled adolescents’ behavior and way of thinking should be in place—giving them a chance to turn their life around (given they have many more years to grow) can allow for change without added frustration and bills.

comments.name: Ashlyn H.
comments.body: Law enforcement being present in schools is necessary for the safety of students, staff, and teachers. I feel safe when I am present in our high school building, but being an early college student, there are times on the college campus that don’t feel secure enough. With young and even older adults wandering around campus, there have been numerous situations of people feeling like they're being followed, being hit on through catcalling, and even just approaching us with no distinct reason. Our high school building is good at settling issues before they become out of control, but that doesn’t mean that it's perfect. There are still police officers walking through our hallways to ensure the safety of every individual within a classroom. In traditional high schools I do believe that law enforcement should be more present because then they can better identify the kids who may need help getting out of their home situations instead of being placed in the cycle of becoming future criminals. As much as teachers and law enforcement want to help kids become better humans, it starts with what they want for themselves and working on breaking the cycle of negative behavior before it's too late.

Being a Scythophile I was surprised at no mention of the Scythian culture, which roamed and fought over the nomad steppe from what is now Hungary in the west all the way to Mongolia and northern China in the east, from the 9th century BCE to about the 2nd century CE. They essentially invented the nomad culture. 

One of the interesting stories that Herodotus tells, is how Darius the 1st, of Persia, tried to do battle with the Scythians of the Pontic Steppe who retreated before him, leading him far north of the Danube and his supply lines. When the Scythians did turn for battle, a rabbit started up between the opposing forces and the Scythians chased off after the rabbit, leaving Darius to comment how the Scythians had no regard for him and his army, whatever. Darius then retreated back to the Danube and parts south.

The story may be apocryphal, but it does illustrate how nomad cultures on the steppes were fiercely competitive when mounted use of bow, spear or axe, were involved.

Thank you for this story.

Thank you for reporting on this Ebola outbreak. Climate change impacts have significantly exacerbated Ebola transmission in Africa through interconnected ecological, economic, and human factors. 

Shifting weather patterns, intensified droughts, and sudden heavy rainfall alter natural ecosystems, disrupting food sources for viral reservoir hosts such as fruit bats. 

As changing microclimates and deforestation force wild animals closer to agricultural zones and rural communities in search of sustenance, animal-to-human spillover events become substantially more frequent.   

Simultaneously, severe climate disruptions cause crop failures, resource scarcity, and water shortages, driving economic distress and agricultural displacement. 

Families are compelled to migrate toward densely populated urban centers or venture deeper into forests for bushmeat hunting and logging, creating high-risk transmission pathways. 

These climate-driven pressures strain fragile healthcare systems and fuel human mobility, accelerating spread.

comments.body: America’s Strategic Petroleum Reserves (SPR) have a capacity of 714 million barrels.  Current reserves now stand at 282 million barrels, its lowest point in over 40 years, since 1982 (when the reserves were just getting built). The Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve is separate from the SPR. It was created under President Clinton to be used for emergencies. It’s been used once, as a result of Hurricane Sandy, but never to try to reduce prices. It has a capacity of 1 million barrels, so this effort will reduce the reserves by 1/3rd.  One thing that might make oil distributors weary of borrowing from these reserves is that they must replace whatever they take, so if home heating oil is even more expensive next year, they will be on the hook for the difference. If the Iran and Houthi wars aren’t successfully concluded, and US refining capacity isn’t increased, and/or if some actual emergency or especially cold winter arises, they could lose a lot of money.

I know it’s kind of a running joke how much we like our protests in France, but in truth it really is something we hold quite sacred, and value very deeply.  No matter the message or affiliation, we will defend everyone’s right to gather and protest, it is enshrined in our constitution and deeply ingrained in each of us.  

There is a provision in the constitution about protests not interfering with rule of law, so the move is not unconstitutional.  I’m a big fan of rule of law, and I want all of the protesters safe.  That said, to ban gatherings outright, even in the wake of recent events, is nonetheless an aggressive move. comments.body: Thanks for the memories, and bless those who keep the Folklife  Festival alive in its newest iteration. May it thrive in some form as long as this country survives, as one of the last examples of the joy we experienced as we celebrated our diversity. I was at the first Festival in 1967. I attended every one through 1981, which is the year I left Washington, DC. Every day of each Festival was filled with gloriously rich and moving moments of connection through music, food, stories, rituals, and crafts. I treasure such vivid memories of a time and a place that no longer exist. Thanks be to Clifford Murphy and others who work to continue the joy of sharing during this current era of mistrust and partisan division.

comments.body: My wife gets in to recommend "The Minx" before it leaves Netflix: "If you like shows with strong female characters and that are set in an interesting historical context, The Minx is for you.  The main character, who is thoughtful and honest, but a bit naive, takes on navigating a world full of soft-core porn and strong personalities in the L.A.Basin in the 1970's while doggedly pursuing her dream of publishing a women's magazine by women and for women.  She holds to her values while having to compromise around the edges to make her dream happen, all within a series of very funny situations that arise (heh!) with her publisher, a strong and ultimately upright entrepreneur  who mentors her through handling the conflicts between her values and the marketplace where she's operating. I'm not making it sound as funny and light-hearted and innocently raunchy as it is.  There's also lots of delightful man-candy women (and men) can enjoy in the scenes set in the publisher's headquarters.  I enjoyed it tremendously while rooting for the characters to get what they need.  Like most contemporary workplace comedies, there are few villains and a whole raft of people just trying to do their best, often with very funny results.  If you liked The Good Place or Community, this may be your jam."
